title: Graft back
hook: a branch cut from its neighbor is cut from the whole tree, but we can be grafted back (Meditations 11.8)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus remembered Homer: the generations of people come and go like leaves in the wind. Your line was like leaves. Did you catch anything moving in the breeze? Day two hundred eighteen.

Scroll far enough down a contact list and there may be a name that's gone quiet for years. Nobody fought. Maybe there was one small sting, a missed wedding, a comment that landed wrong, and then it was easier to not reply. Then easier again. Now the gap feels too big to cross, and every month it gets a little bigger. Gardeners know something about this. You can cut a branch off an apple tree and, with a clean cut and a little binding, fit it back onto living wood, and it grows. That's called grafting. Marcus Aurelius borrows the gardeners' picture. Today, graft back.
screen: `THE NAME YOU HAVEN'T MESSAGED.` → `THE GAP GETS BIGGER.` → `GRAFT BACK.`

segments.voice: Book eleven of the Meditations. Marcus is looking at a tree. In George Long's 1862 translation: "A branch cut off from the adjacent branch must of necessity be cut off from the whole tree also." You can't be cut from your neighbor without being cut from everything the neighbor is part of. For Marcus, a person belongs to a great shared community, the whole human city, and falling out with one person is falling a little way out of all of it. Then comes the twist. A branch doesn't cut itself off. Someone else takes the saw to it. But a person, Marcus says, does it alone, by hating someone and turning away, and doesn't even notice that he's cut himself off from the whole. That's the hard part. Then comes the reason for today. Marcus says we have a gift the branch doesn't: we can grow back to the one near us, and become part of the whole again. Graft back. And then, being Marcus, he adds a caution. If the cutting happens again and again, the joining gets harder. The gardeners say a branch that grew with the tree isn't quite the same as one grafted back after being cut. So don't make a habit of the saw. Think about what a real graft needs. A clean cut, not a ragged one. The two living surfaces pressed close. Something to bind them. And time, while the wood knits. That's not a bad description of reconnecting with a person. A simple, honest message. Actually showing up. Patience while it heals.
screen: `CUT FROM ONE, CUT FROM THE WHOLE.` · `A PERSON CUTS HIMSELF OFF.` · `WE CAN GROW BACK.` · `CLEAN CUT, BOUND CLOSE, TIME.` · then, large: `GRAFT BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reconnect with one person, starting right here. Settle and breathe. Let one name come, someone you've drifted from without a real reason. Not someone who hurt you badly. Some cuts are right to keep. Just a drift. Picture their face. Notice what's in the gap: pride, awkwardness, simple time. Then picture the first plain sentence you could send. Thought of you today. How are you? Hold it gently. The bell holds the time.
Graft back. Marcus's picture of a branch rejoining the tree: cut from one person, you're cut from the whole, and you can grow back. Today's word.
Your line: graft back. Today, send the plain sentence to the person who came to mind. No long apology needed, just the plain sentence and the reaching. Day two hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often take Meditations 11.8 as a prompt to repair a drifted relationship: one short, honest message rather than waiting for the perfect moment.

fork.setup: you've drifted from a friend for two years. no fight, just silence. what does Marcus's tree suggest?
options: wait for them to go first.
let it go; the branch is gone.
fork.reveal: Marcus says a person has a gift the branch lacks: we can grow back to our neighbor. he also warns not to make the cutting a habit.

what a scholar hears: Meditations 11.8, the Stoic idea of one shared human city; Marcus credits Zeus, who framed society, with the power to grow back.
